concept: Caching (exact-match memoization, semantic caching, prompt/prefix caching, KV reuse, invalidation)
summary:
Caching for LLM pipelines is now a four-layer stack, each layer validated by a distinct literature. (1) Exact-match response memoization is classical systems engineering: canonical key construction (normalized text, canonical JSON, cryptographic hash chained over the prefix, versioned namespaces) borrowed directly from vLLM's block-hash design (parent hash + token ids + extra keys, sha256 default, cache_salt for tenant isolation), with eviction/admission governed by the 60-year-old replacement-policy canon (Belady's OPT 1966 as the offline bound; LRU; ARC 2003 self-tuning recency/frequency; W-TinyLFU 2017 frequency-based admission) and operational hygiene from web caching (XFetch probabilistic early expiration against stampedes, VLDB 2015; negative caching with bounded TTL, RFC 2308). (2) Semantic caching (GPTCache, NLP-OSS 2023, ~8.2k GitHub stars; MeanCache, IPDPS 2025; SCALM 2024; GPT Semantic Cache 2024) returns a stored answer when a new prompt's embedding is close to a stored one, yielding 2-10x faster hits and 60-69% API-call reductions on repetitive workloads, but the literature is equally clear on the central risk: generic embeddings predict "same answer" poorly (AUC 0.51 on a hard NQ-derived set, Zhu et al. 2024), static thresholds give unpredictable false-hit rates, and the state of the art (vCache, ICLR 2026) replaces one global threshold with per-entry online-learned thresholds under a user-specified error bound (up to 12.5x higher hit rate and 26x lower error than static thresholds). (3) Provider-side prompt/prefix caching (Anthropic: 5-min write 1.25x, 1-hour write 2x, reads 0.1x base price, up to 4 breakpoints, 20-position automatic lookback, 512-4096 token minimums by model; OpenAI: 1,024-token minimum, 1.25x write/0.1x read on recent models, 30-minute TTL) makes prefix stability a first-class design constraint: static content first, dynamic content last, no timestamps in the prefix, and awareness that tool-definition, image, thinking/effort changes invalidate the cache. (4) KV-cache reuse inside the serving engine (vLLM PagedAttention, SOSP 2023; SGLang RadixAttention, NeurIPS 2024, up to 6.4x throughput; Prompt Cache modular reuse, MLSys 2024, 8x GPU/60x CPU TTFT; ChunkAttention, ACL 2024, 3.2-4.8x kernel speedup; Hydragen shared-prefix attention, up to 32x throughput; CacheBlend non-prefix fusion, EuroSys 2025 best paper, 2.2-3.3x TTFT; CacheGen KV compression, SIGCOMM 2024, 3.5-4.3x smaller; RAGCache, up to 4x TTFT) removes recomputation of shared prefixes and, increasingly, of non-prefix retrieved chunks.

The production implication is that a caching component must be a policy engine rather than a dictionary: it must decide per request which layers apply (exact, semantic, provider-prefix, engine-KV), construct keys that encode every determinant of the output (model id, prompt-template version, tool schema hash, sampling params, retrieval snapshot), bound the semantic false-hit rate explicitly, coalesce concurrent misses, and expose hit rate, false-hit rate, tokens/cost saved, p50/p99 TTFT, and staleness as first-class metrics. For engineering workloads (code, specs, standards, requirements, test logs, incident reports, CAD/BOM metadata) the dominant adaptations are: treat identifiers and numeric tolerances as exact-match guards on top of embedding similarity, pin cache entries to document/corpus versions for dependency-based invalidation, and exploit the very long, very stable reference material (standards, spec sections, schemas) through 1-hour provider prefix caching and engine-side KV reuse.

papers.title: GPTCache: An Open-Source Semantic Cache for LLM Applications Enabling Faster Answers and Cost Savings
papers.authors: Fu Bang
papers.citation_signal: Reference open-source semantic cache; GitHub repository zilliztech/GPTCache shows ~8.2k stars and ~600 forks; integrated into LangChain/LlamaIndex ecosystems; used as the baseline by SCALM, MeanCache, vCache and others.
papers.key_contribution: Describes a modular semantic cache (LLM adapter, embedding generator, cache storage, vector store, similarity evaluator, eviction manager with LRU/FIFO/LFU/RR) that intercepts LLM API calls and returns stored responses when a query is similar enough to a cached one. Integrated with OpenAI's GPT service it increases response speed 2-10x on cache hits and decouples response time from network fluctuations. The README exposes a configurable similarity_threshold and a 'temperature' knob (0-2, default 0) that probabilistically bypasses the cache to preserve response diversity.
papers.design_implication: Adopt GPTCache's separation of concerns as the reference architecture: pluggable embedding, pluggable vector index, pluggable scalar store, a separate similarity-evaluation stage, and a pluggable eviction policy. Do not adopt its documented weakness: eviction counts entries rather than bytes and can OOM, so a production component must do size-aware eviction. Keep a temperature-style bypass knob for tasks that need diversity (brainstorming) versus determinism (spec lookup).

papers.title: MeanCache: User-Centric Semantic Caching for LLM Web Services
papers.authors: Waris Gill, Mohamed Elidrisi, Pallavi Kalapatapu, Ammar Ahmed, Ali Anwar, Muhammad Ali Gulzar
papers.citation_signal: Top-tier parallel/distributed systems venue (IPDPS); Semantic Scholar shows ~20 citations; Cisco and Virginia Tech co-authorship signals industry relevance.
papers.key_contribution: Reports that about 31% of LLM queries are repeats, motivating caching. Proposes a user-side semantic cache that trains its similarity model via federated learning (no raw query sharing) and stores context chains with each entry so contextual (multi-turn) queries are not confused with standalone ones. Against the state-of-the-art cache (GPTCache) it reports ~17% higher F-score and ~20% higher precision on hit/miss decisions, 83% lower storage, and 11% faster hit/miss decisions.
papers.design_implication: Semantic keys must include conversational context (a hash or embedding of the preceding turns), not just the latest message; otherwise follow-up queries produce false hits. Precision (false-hit avoidance), not just hit rate, is the headline metric. Where data sensitivity matters (incident reports, proprietary designs) keep the semantic cache close to the user/tenant and train or tune the similarity model without centralizing raw prompts.

papers.title: Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency Inference
papers.authors: In Gim, Guojun Chen, Seung-seob Lee, Nikhil Sarda, Anurag Khandelwal, Lin Zhong
papers.citation_signal: Peer-reviewed at MLSys 2024; widely cited as the origin of schema-driven, position-aware KV reuse for non-contiguous prompt modules; precursor to CacheBlend-style non-prefix reuse.
papers.key_contribution: Precomputes and stores attention (KV) states for frequently reused text segments ('prompt modules': system messages, templates, reference documents) defined by a schema, and reuses them when they appear in user prompts, with position handling so reuse stays accurate. Reduces time-to-first-token by 8x on GPU and up to 60x on CPU inference for long prompts (document QA, recommendation) with no loss of output accuracy and no parameter changes.
papers.design_implication: Treat prompts as compositions of named, versioned modules (system instructions, tool specs, standard clauses, spec sections) and make the module boundaries explicit so both provider-side prefix caching and self-hosted KV reuse can key on them. A schema/template registry with content hashes per module is the shared substrate for exact-match, prefix, and KV caching.

papers.title: SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (RadixAttention)
papers.authors: Lianmin Zheng, Liangsheng Yin, Zhiqiang Xie, Chuyue Sun, Jeff Huang, Cody Hao Yu, Shiyi Cao, Christos Kozyrakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Clark Barrett, Ying Sheng
papers.citation_signal: NeurIPS 2024 main track; Semantic Scholar shows ~1,600 citations; SGLang is a production inference engine with broad industry adoption.
papers.key_contribution: Introduces RadixAttention: the KV cache of all prompts and generations is kept in a radix tree keyed by token sequences (values are paged GPU KV tensors), with LRU eviction of leaf nodes and a cache-aware scheduling policy that raises hit rate; the tree lives on CPU with negligible overhead so it is always on. Combined with compressed finite-state machines for structured decoding, SGLang achieves up to 6.4x higher throughput than state-of-the-art systems across agent control, reasoning, few-shot, JSON decoding, RAG, and multi-turn chat; the LMSYS blog reports up to 5x over vLLM/Guidance/TGI on Llama-7B and Mixtral-8x7B.
papers.design_implication: If you self-host, use an engine with automatic radix/prefix KV caching and let your pipeline exploit it by (a) keeping shared prefixes byte-identical and (b) scheduling requests that share prefixes together (cache-aware ordering of fan-out calls). Tree-structured workloads (task decomposition, tree-of-thought, self-consistency) are exactly where radix reuse pays.

papers.title: CacheBlend: Fast Large Language Model Serving for RAG with Cached Knowledge Fusion
papers.authors: Jiayi Yao, Hanchen Li, Yuhan Liu, Siddhant Ray, Yihua Cheng, Qizheng Zhang, Kuntai Du, Shan Lu, Junchen Jiang
papers.citation_signal: Best Paper at EuroSys 2025 (top systems venue); implemented in LMCache, which is reported as the KV caching layer used with Red Hat, IBM, Google and CoreWeave deployments.
papers.key_contribution: Shows that precomputed KV caches only help when reused text is a prefix; otherwise cross-attention with preceding text is lost. CacheBlend reuses precomputed KV for arbitrary (non-prefix) chunks by selectively recomputing KV for a small subset of tokens and pipelining that recomputation with KV retrieval from slower storage. On three open LLMs and four benchmarks it cuts TTFT by 2.2-3.3x and raises throughput 2.8-5x versus full prefill with no quality loss.
papers.design_implication: For RAG-heavy engineering pipelines where retrieved chunks arrive in varying order, per-chunk KV caching with blend-style partial recompute removes the need to force a fixed chunk order for prefix hits. Store chunk KV in a tiered store (GPU -> CPU -> SSD) and treat it as a cache with its own eviction and versioning tied to the corpus snapshot.

papers.title: CacheGen: KV Cache Compression and Streaming for Fast Large Language Model Serving
papers.authors: Yuhan Liu, Hanchen Li, Yihua Cheng, Siddhant Ray, Yuyang Huang, Qizheng Zhang, Kuntai Du, Jiayi Yao, Shan Lu, Ganesh Ananthanarayanan, Michael Maire, Henry Hoffmann, Ari Holtzman, Junchen Jiang
papers.citation_signal: SIGCOMM 2024 (top networking venue); Microsoft co-authorship; foundational for the LMCache project's KV offload/transfer layer.
papers.key_contribution: Observes that reusing a stored KV cache for long contexts saves prefill but moving multi-GB KV tensors over the network adds its own delay. A custom tensor encoder exploiting KV distributional properties produces compact bitstreams with negligible decode cost and adapts compression level to available bandwidth. Versus KV-reuse baselines it shrinks KV size 3.5-4.3x and reduces total context fetch+process delay 3.2-3.7x with negligible quality impact.
papers.design_implication: A distributed KV cache (multi-node or cross-region) must budget transfer time against recompute time; compress and stream KV, and fall back to recompute when bandwidth is poor. Expose a cost model (bytes, bandwidth, prefill FLOPs) so the component can choose per request between fetching cached KV and recomputing.

papers.title: Hydragen: High-Throughput LLM Inference with Shared Prefixes
papers.authors: Jordan Juravsky, Bradley Brown, Ryan Ehrlich, Daniel Y. Fu, Christopher Ré, Azalia Mirhoseini
papers.citation_signal: Stanford Scaling Intelligence Lab; Semantic Scholar shows ~95 citations; the shared-prefix attention decomposition it introduced is now used in production attention kernels.
papers.key_contribution: In large batches that share a prefix (few-shot examples, system prompt), decoding is attention-bound by repeated KV reads. Hydragen computes exact attention over the shared prefix once (batched queries, matrix-matrix products) and over each unique suffix separately. End-to-end CodeLlama-13b throughput improves up to 32x; growing the prefix from 1K to 16K tokens costs Hydragen <15% throughput while baselines lose >90%; tree-structured sharing cuts competitive-programming inference time 55%.
papers.design_implication: When the pipeline fans out N parallel samples or N sub-tasks over the same long context (specs, standards, code files), batch them to the same engine so shared-prefix attention applies; this makes long shared context nearly free at the decode stage, not just at prefill. Design the parallelization layer to group calls by prefix hash.

papers.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (vLLM)
papers.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica
papers.citation_signal: SOSP 2023 (top systems venue); Semantic Scholar shows ~9,000 citations; vLLM is the most widely deployed open-source LLM serving engine.
papers.key_contribution: Introduces PagedAttention, an OS-virtual-memory-inspired KV layout that reduces KV cache waste to near-zero and enables flexible KV sharing within and across requests. vLLM improves throughput 2-4x at the same latency versus FasterTransformer and Orca, with gains growing for longer sequences, larger models, and complex decoding. Its automatic prefix caching (per the vLLM design docs) hashes each full block as (parent block hash, block token ids, extra keys such as LoRA id, multimodal hashes, cache_salt), defaults to sha256, and evicts via an LRU free-block queue in which a finished request's last blocks are evicted first.
papers.design_implication: The block-hash chain is the canonical model for cache-key design at every layer: each key commits to everything before it plus discriminating 'extra keys'. Use a cryptographic hash by default (the vLLM docs warn non-cryptographic hashes risk collisions and cross-tenant leakage) and add a tenant salt to isolate caches. Note that prefix caching speeds only prefill, so budget expectations accordingly for generation-heavy tasks.

papers.title: A Study of Replacement Algorithms for a Virtual-Storage Computer
papers.authors: László A. Bélády
papers.citation_signal: Foundational classic cited in every OS textbook (e.g., Silberschatz et al. bibliography); defines the OPT/MIN algorithm that remains the offline optimum for cache simulation.
papers.key_contribution: Introduces the optimal (MIN/OPT) replacement rule: evict the item whose next use is furthest in the future, which minimizes misses for a fixed cache size (optimality later proved by Mattson et al. 1970). Also reports that policies favoring recently used pages, LRU in particular, outperform the alternatives tested.
papers.design_implication: Use Belady-OPT as the offline upper bound when evaluating any eviction policy on recorded LLM request traces: the gap between your policy's hit rate and OPT's tells you whether to invest in smarter eviction or in increasing capacity/TTL. Start with LRU (which RadixAttention and vLLM both use) and only move to ARC/TinyLFU if trace replay shows a material gap.

papers.title: ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache
papers.authors: Nimrod Megiddo, Dharmendra S. Modha
papers.citation_signal: Top storage venue; the basis of ZFS's adaptive replacement cache and of PostgreSQL/IBM storage controllers; thousands of citations.
papers.key_contribution: ARC maintains two LRU lists (recently used once, T1; used at least twice, T2) plus ghost lists of evicted keys and adaptively moves the partition point p based on ghost hits, balancing recency and frequency online with constant time per request and no workload-specific tuning. It is scan-resistant and on 23 real traces substantially beats LRU; on an SPC1-like benchmark at 4 GB it reports 20% hit ratio versus 9.19% for LRU.
papers.design_implication: For response caches that see both bursty repeated queries and one-off scans (e.g., bulk log analysis), ARC-style adaptivity prevents one-time requests from flushing valuable entries without hand-tuned parameters. Implement ghost lists keyed by hash so the memory overhead is small.

papers.title: TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy
papers.authors: Gil Einziger, Roy Friedman, Ben Manes
papers.venue: ACM Transactions on Storage 13(4), Article 35 (arXiv 1512.00727; earlier version Euromicro PDP 2014)
papers.citation_signal: ACM TOS journal; W-TinyLFU is the default policy of the Caffeine Java cache (Ben Manes), used by Cassandra, Druid and many JVM services; routinely top of hit-ratio benchmarks.
papers.key_contribution: Proposes admission filtering: a new item is admitted only if its approximate recent frequency (TinyLFU, a compact Bloom-filter-style sketch with aging) exceeds that of the eviction victim. W-TinyLFU pairs a small LRU window with a main segmented-LRU region guarded by the TinyLFU filter and achieves hit ratios equal to or better than state-of-the-art policies across the evaluated traces.
papers.design_implication: LLM response and KV caches are capacity-constrained and skewed; an admission filter keeps one-off prompts from displacing hot ones (important when expensive KV entries are large). Use a frequency sketch keyed by the exact-match hash so the policy is cheap and works across semantic and exact layers.

papers.title: Prompt caching (Claude Developer Platform documentation)
papers.authors: Anthropic
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation defining the state of practice for provider-side prefix caching economics and semantics.
papers.key_contribution: Defines the economics and semantics of provider-side prefix caching: 5-minute cache writes cost 1.25x base input, 1-hour writes 2x, cache reads 0.1x (0.05x and 0.025x on the newest models); TTL is measured from request start and refreshed free on every hit; minimum cacheable length is 512, 1,024, 2,048 or 4,096 tokens depending on model; prefix is matched in the order tools -> system -> messages up to a cache_control breakpoint; up to 4 breakpoints per request; the system automatically looks back up to 20 block positions per breakpoint; changes to tool definitions invalidate everything, image changes invalidate tools+system, thinking/effort settings invalidate message blocks; a cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins, so parallel requests must wait for the first to start; usage reports cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens; caches are isolated per organization/workspace and never shared across organizations.
papers.design_implication: Prefix stability is a design constraint: place one breakpoint at the end of the last block that is identical across requests, never on a block that varies (timestamps, user input). Break-even is immediate: with write 1.25x and read 0.1x, the second use within TTL already saves money (1.25 + 0.1 < 2.0); the 1-hour TTL (2x write) pays off from the third use, so pick TTL from the observed inter-arrival distribution of reuses. Serialize the first request before fanning out parallel calls, and monitor cache_read_input_tokens / total input tokens as the hit-rate metric.

papers.title: Prompt caching (OpenAI API documentation)
papers.authors: OpenAI
papers.citation_signal: Authoritative provider documentation; the second major provider's prefix-caching contract, useful for provider-agnostic design.
papers.key_contribution: Automatic prefix caching with a 1,024-token minimum on recent models; cached input discounted up to 95% (reads 0.1x, writes 1.25x on recent models; 0.05x reads on the newest); retention of about 5-10 minutes of inactivity up to an hour for in-memory entries, an extended retention option, and a 30-minute TTL on the newest models; cache reuse requires the entire rendered prefix to match and lookups try longest eligible prefix first; prompt_cache_key influences routing (does not guarantee a hit) and provides per-customer cache accounting; cached_tokens is reported in usage (rounded down to 128 on older models). Best practices: put stable developer instructions and shared reference material first, dynamic content such as timestamps last, and append rather than rewrite messages because summarization/compaction resets reuse.

Treat conversation compaction as a cache-invalidating event and schedule it deliberately.

papers.title: GPT Semantic Cache: Reducing LLM Costs and Latency via Semantic Embedding Caching
papers.authors: Sajal Regmi, Chetan Phakami Pun
papers.citation_signal: Semantic Scholar shows ~32 citations within about a year; frequently cited as the Redis-based reference design for semantic caching in customer-service settings.
papers.key_contribution: Stores query embeddings in Redis and returns pre-generated responses for semantically similar queries. Reports API-call reductions of up to 68.8% across query categories, cache hit rates of 61.6% to 68.8%, and 'positive hit rates' (hits judged correct) above 97% on repetitive customer-service style queries.
papers.design_implication: On FAQ-like, highly repetitive workloads, semantic caching can remove two thirds of LLM calls; the ~3% incorrect-hit residue is the number a verifier or a tighter threshold must drive down. Use an in-memory vector store (Redis/HNSW) for sub-millisecond lookups and log the 'positive hit rate' via sampled human/LLM judgement.

papers.title: SCALM: Towards Semantic Caching for Automated Chat Services with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jiaxing Li, Chi Xu, Feng Wang, Isaac M. von Riedemann, Cong Zhang, Jiangchuan Liu
papers.venue: arXiv 2406.00025 (reported as IEEE/ACM IWQoS 2024 by citing works; venue not confirmed on arXiv page)
papers.citation_signal: Analysis grounded in real human-LLM interaction traces (LMSYS, MOSS); widely cited in the 2025 semantic-caching literature as the first semantic-aware storage/eviction design.
papers.key_contribution: Analyzes real-world human-to-LLM chat data and finds existing caches ignore semantic connections between queries. SCALM clusters queries semantically to identify significant cache entries and patterns and adds matching storage and eviction strategies. Versus GPTCache it reports an average 63% relative increase in cache hit ratio and 77% relative improvement in token savings; semantic eviction strategies alone give 35-38% token-saving improvements and enhanced preprocessing 46-48% over an LFU baseline.
papers.design_implication: Eviction for a semantic cache should rank by cluster-level value (how many distinct queries an entry serves, tokens saved per hit) rather than per-entry recency alone; preprocessing/normalization of queries is worth as much as the eviction policy. Build a query-level trace simulator to evaluate policies offline before deployment.

papers.title: Efficient Prompt Caching via Embedding Similarity
papers.authors: Hanlin Zhu, Banghua Zhu, Jiantao Jiao
papers.citation_signal: UC Berkeley theory group; provides the finite-sample guarantees and the clearest quantitative evidence that off-the-shelf embeddings mis-predict cache validity; cited by vCache and follow-on work.
papers.key_contribution: Shows that semantic similarity is not the same as 'the same response answers both prompts': on a hard dataset derived from Natural Questions, an existing embedding model (Wang et al. 2022) achieves only AUC 0.51 (chance) at predicting whether caching is valid. A distillation-based fine-tuning of the embedding raises AUC to 0.81, with finite-sample convergence guarantees for several loss types, and simulations show better caching efficiency.
papers.design_implication: Never deploy a semantic cache on general-purpose embeddings with a hand-picked threshold without measuring AUC on labeled 'same-answer' pairs from your own domain. Fine-tune or distill the embedding toward response equivalence, and for engineering text add exact-match guards on identifiers and numbers that embeddings blur.

papers.title: vCache: Verified Semantic Prompt Caching
papers.authors: Luis Gaspar Schroeder, Aditya Desai, Alejandro Cuadron, Kyle Chu, Shu Liu, Mark Zhao, Stephan Krusche, Alfons Kemper, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez
papers.venue: ICLR 2026 (arXiv 2502.03771, v1 Feb 2025) | also known as: vCache: Verified Semantic Prompt Caching (earlier title: Adaptive Semantic Prompt Caching with VectorQ)
papers.citation_signal: Accepted at ICLR 2026 (top ML venue); UC Berkeley/TUM; releases an open implementation and four semantic-caching benchmarks that are becoming the standard evaluation suite.
papers.key_contribution: Argues that a single static similarity threshold gives no correctness guarantee, unpredictable error rates and sub-optimal hit rates. vCache lets the user specify a maximum error rate and uses an online learning algorithm (no extra training) to estimate an optimal threshold per cached prompt. It consistently meets the specified error bound and achieves up to 12.5x higher cache hit rates and 26x lower error rates than static-threshold and fine-tuned-embedding baselines.
papers.design_implication: Make the semantic cache's contract an error budget (e.g., 'at most 2% incorrect hits') rather than a cosine threshold; learn per-entry thresholds online from observed hit correctness (which the pipeline's verification component can supply). Ship the four vCache benchmarks plus domain-specific labeled pairs as the regression suite.

papers.title: RAGCache: Efficient Knowledge Caching for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.authors: Chao Jin, Zili Zhang, Xuanlin Jiang, Fangyue Liu, Xin Liu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin
papers.citation_signal: Peking University/ByteDance; among the most cited RAG-serving systems papers of 2024 and the first to formalize KV caching of retrieved documents as a multilevel knowledge tree.
papers.key_contribution: Benchmarks RAG serving and identifies long knowledge-injected inputs as the bottleneck. RAGCache caches intermediate (KV) states of retrieved documents in a knowledge tree spanning GPU and host memory, with a replacement policy aware of both LLM inference cost and RAG retrieval patterns, and overlaps retrieval with inference. On vLLM + Faiss it reduces TTFT by up to 4x and improves throughput up to 2.1x.
papers.design_implication: In a pipeline-RAG component, the retrieved-document KV cache should be tiered (GPU hot, CPU warm) with a cost-aware eviction policy (recompute cost x access frequency), and retrieval should be overlapped with speculative prefill of the stable prefix. Key cached document states by (document id, chunk id, corpus version, model id).

papers.title: ChunkAttention: Efficient Self-Attention with Prefix-Aware KV Cache and Two-Phase Partition
papers.authors: Lu Ye, Ze Tao, Yong Huang, Yang Li
papers.citation_signal: ACL 2024 main conference (top NLP venue); Microsoft authorship; independent confirmation of prefix-tree KV sharing with kernel-level gains.
papers.key_contribution: In multi-tenant serving with shared system prompts, ChunkAttention detects matching prefixes at runtime, chunks KV tensors and stores them once in a prefix tree, and uses a two-phase partition kernel for locality. The self-attention kernel runs 3.2-4.8x faster than the prior state of the art for system prompts of 1,024-4,096 tokens.
papers.design_implication: Long shared system prompts (company style guides, safety rules, engineering standards) are an asset rather than a cost when the serving stack dedupes them; standardize on a small number of long, byte-stable system prompts per task family instead of many slightly different ones.

papers.title: Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention
papers.authors: Andrea Vattani, Flavio Chierichetti, Keegan Lowenstein
papers.citation_signal: VLDB (top database venue); the XFetch algorithm it defines is implemented in production cache libraries (e.g., Rust xfetch crate, Redis community guidance) and referenced in the Wikipedia 'cache stampede' entry.
papers.key_contribution: When a hot entry expires, many concurrent requests recompute it simultaneously (stampede / thundering herd). The paper gives provably optimal probabilistic early-expiration algorithms: each reader recomputes early when now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry, where delta is the measured recompute cost stored with the entry and beta (default 1.0) tunes eagerness; expensive entries are refreshed earlier, no locks or coordination are needed, and the method performs much better than solutions used in practice.
papers.design_implication: LLM recomputation is slow (seconds) and expensive, so stampedes are costly; store the last generation latency with each entry and apply XFetch with beta=1 for hot keys, combined with single-flight request coalescing for cold misses. The same logic applies to warming provider prefix caches before a burst.

papers.title: RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries (DNS NCACHE)
papers.authors: Mark Andrews
papers.citation_signal: Internet standard implemented by every DNS resolver; the canonical specification of negative caching and bounded negative TTLs.
papers.key_contribution: Specifies caching of negative answers (name does not exist / no data) so repeated misses are answered locally, with the negative TTL set to the smaller of the SOA TTL and SOA MINIMUM, a resolver-side cap on negative TTL that should not exceed the positive cap, 'values of one to three hours have been found to work well', and a warning that values over one day caused problems.
papers.design_implication: Cache 'no result' outcomes (retrieval returned nothing relevant, verifier rejected, tool returned not-found) with a short, bounded TTL so repeated failing queries do not re-run the expensive pipeline, but keep negative TTLs well below positive TTLs and tie them to corpus/index versions so newly ingested documents become visible promptly.

papers.title: Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving: From Offline Learning to Online Adaptation
papers.authors: Xutong Liu, Baran Atalar, Xiangxiang Dai, Jinhang Zuo, Siwei Wang, John C.S. Lui, Wei Chen, Carlee Joe-Wong
papers.citation_signal: INFOCOM 2026 (top networking venue); CMU/CUHK/Microsoft Research; the first formal treatment of semantic-cache eviction with mismatch costs and provable guarantees.
papers.key_contribution: Generalizes exact-match caching by adding a mismatch cost for serving a semantically similar but different cached response, formulates semantic cache eviction as offline optimization and online learning under unknown query and cost distributions, and gives algorithms with provable efficiency guarantees that match or beat baselines on a synthetic dataset.
papers.design_implication: Model each semantic hit as (benefit = cost of LLM call saved) minus (expected mismatch cost), and let eviction and admission maximize net value rather than raw hit rate. Mismatch cost should be domain-configured: near zero for FAQ paraphrases, very high for engineering tolerances, part numbers, or safety-critical requirements.

papers.title: An Ensemble Embedding Approach for Improving Semantic Caching Performance in LLM-based Systems
papers.authors: Shervin Ghaffari, Zohre Bahranifard, Mohammad Akbari
papers.venue: arXiv 2507.07061 (submitted to Journal of Information Science)
papers.citation_signal: Recent preprint (lower-rated than the others; included as corroborating evidence on embedding choice, not as a primary source).
papers.key_contribution: Combines multiple embedding models through a trained meta-encoder for semantic cache matching. On Quora Question Pairs it reports a 92% cache hit ratio for semantically equivalent queries and 85% accuracy in rejecting non-equivalent queries as misses, outperforming single-model embeddings.
papers.design_implication: Embedding choice is a tunable component; an ensemble or domain-adapted embedding can materially raise both recall and rejection accuracy. Keep the embedding model id in the cache key namespace so that swapping embeddings invalidates the semantic index cleanly.

papers.title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Ruoyu Qin, Zheming Li, Weiran He, Jialei Cui, Feng Ren, Mingxing Zhang, Yongwei Wu, Weimin Zheng, Xinran Xu
papers.venue: USENIX FAST 2025, pp. 155-170, Best Paper Award (arXiv 2407.00079, v1 Jun 2024) | also known as: Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation - A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (arXiv title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving)
papers.citation_signal: FAST 2025 Best Paper (Erik Riedel award, confirmed on the USENIX presentation page); production system behind Moonshot AI's Kimi, deployed across thousands of nodes processing over 100 billion tokens/day; open-source Mooncake/Transfer Engine adopted by vLLM and SGLang ecosystems.
papers.key_contribution: Treats the KV cache as the first-class, disaggregated resource of an LLM serving cluster: prefill and decode run on separate pools, and the KV cache lives in a distributed store built from otherwise idle CPU DRAM, SSD and RDMA NICs, with a KVCache-centric scheduler that trades storage for recomputation under latency SLOs. On real traces it raises effective request capacity by 59%-498% versus baselines while meeting SLOs; the arXiv version reports up to 525% throughput in simulation and 75% more requests handled by Kimi; the FAST version reports 115%/107% more requests on A800/H800 clusters.
papers.design_implication: The dossier treats engine-side KV reuse as a single-node concern (radix tree in one engine). At production scale the KV cache is a cluster-wide, tiered, network-attached store with its own placement, replication and eviction policy, and the router must be KV-aware (send a request where its prefix KV already lives, or decide to recompute when transfer is slower). The component's L4 layer should therefore expose a 'where is this prefix cached' lookup and a transfer-vs-recompute cost model rather than assuming co-location.
papers.verification_evidence: arXiv 2407.00079: same work; dossier used an alternate/journal title (Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation - A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (arXiv title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving)); normalised to the arXiv title

papers.title: Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Serving for Multi-turn Conversations with CachedAttention
papers.authors: Bin Gao, Zhuomin He, Puru Sharma, Qingxuan Kang, Djordje Jevdjic, Junbo Deng, Xingkun Yang, Zhou Yu, Pengfei Zuo
papers.citation_signal: Top systems venue (ATC); NUS/SJTU/Huawei Cloud; the standard reference for cross-turn KV persistence and the first to quantify the repetitive prefill cost in multi-turn chat (up to 99% of prefill on ShareGPT per the paper).
papers.key_contribution: Serving engines discard a session's KV cache when the conversation goes idle and recompute it from scratch on the next turn. CachedAttention keeps KV caches in a hierarchical store (HBM -> host DRAM -> disk) across turns, with layer-wise pre-loading and asynchronous saving to overlap I/O with GPU compute, scheduler-aware prefetching and eviction, and position-encoding decoupling so cached KV survives context truncation. Reports up to 87% lower TTFT, up to 7.8x higher prefill throughput for multi-turn conversations, and up to 70% lower end-to-end inference cost.
papers.design_implication: Multi-turn sessions (agent loops, long engineering review threads) should pin per-session KV in a tiered store keyed by (session id, model id, token-prefix hash) with explicit idle-time eviction rather than relying on the engine's in-GPU LRU, and the prefetch of a session's KV should be triggered when the user starts typing or when the orchestrator schedules the next step. Context truncation/compaction must be position-aware or it destroys the cached KV; this is the self-hosted analogue of the provider-side 'compaction resets the cache' pitfall.

papers.title: EPIC: Efficient Position-Independent Caching for Serving Large Language Models
papers.authors: Junhao Hu, Wenrui Huang, Weidong Wang, Haoyi Wang, Tiancheng Hu, Qin Zhang, Hao Feng, Xusheng Chen, Yizhou Shan, Tao Xie
papers.citation_signal: ICML 2025 main conference; Huawei Cloud/PKU; the formalization of 'position-independent caching' (PIC) that generalizes CacheBlend and is being adopted by KV-cache layers for RAG.
papers.key_contribution: Defines Position-Independent Caching: reuse a document's KV regardless of what precedes it. Identifies the per-document 'attention sink' at the start of each independently-encoded chunk as the main source of quality loss and introduces LegoLink (static recomputation of only the first few tokens of each chunk, instead of CacheBlend's dynamic selection), plus chunking that preserves semantic coherence. Reports up to 8x TTFT and 7x throughput improvement over existing systems with negligible or no accuracy loss.
papers.design_implication: For RAG over engineering corpora the chunk-KV layer should recompute a small fixed set of leading tokens per chunk (attention-sink repair) rather than a dynamically-selected subset; this is cheaper and deterministic, which matters for reproducibility and auditability. Chunk boundaries used for KV caching should coincide with semantic boundaries (clauses, sections, functions), not fixed token windows.

papers.title: Preble: Efficient Distributed Prompt Scheduling for LLM Serving
papers.authors: Vikranth Srivatsa, Zijian He, Reyna Abhyankar, Dongming Li, Yiying Zhang
papers.citation_signal: ICLR 2025 main conference; UCSD; the reference work on multi-GPU prefix-aware scheduling, directly addressing the gap between single-engine RadixAttention and distributed serving.
papers.key_contribution: Observes that prior prompt/KV reuse systems (RadixAttention, Prompt Cache, etc.) are single-GPU optimizations while production serving is distributed. Preble co-optimizes KV reuse and load balancing with a hierarchical scheduler: a global scheduler decides which GPU receives a request based on where its prefix is cached versus current load, and local schedulers order requests for locality. Reports 1.5x-14.5x lower average latency and 2x-10x lower p99 latency than SOTA systems on 2-8 GPUs with real workloads.
papers.design_implication: The dossier's advice to 'route requests sharing a prefix to the same engine' needs a policy: Preble's rule is to prefer the engine holding the longest matching prefix unless its load exceeds a threshold, in which case replicate the prefix to a second engine. Implement a global prefix-tree index across replicas (prefix hash -> set of engines holding it) and a load-aware tie-breaker; this is the cache-aware scheduling component the parallelization layer must call.

papers.title: LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
papers.authors: Yuhan Liu, Yihua Cheng, Jiayi Yao, Yuwei An, Xiaokun Chen, Shaoting Feng, Yuyang Huang, Samuel Shen, Rui Zhang, Kuntai Du, Junchen Jiang
papers.citation_signal: MLSys 2026 oral; the system that productizes CacheGen and CacheBlend (both already in the dossier) and is the KV connector integrated with vLLM and SGLang; the dossier mentions LMCache in passing but does not cite the paper.
papers.key_contribution: Describes an engine-external KV cache layer that extracts KV from vLLM/SGLang, stores it across GPU/CPU/disk/remote tiers, and shares it across engines and queries. Supports both offloading (prefix reuse across queries) and prefill-decode disaggregation (cross-engine, cross-GPU KV transfer), and argues KV should be movable, pinnable and compressible through explicit control APIs so routers can make cache-aware decisions. Reports up to 15x throughput improvement with vLLM on multi-round QA and document analysis, and at least 2x lower latency than built-in engine caching and commercial APIs in tested settings.
papers.design_implication: The L4 hooks in the dossier's architecture should target an external KV layer with pin/move/compress APIs rather than engine-internal caches; pinning lets the pipeline keep standards/spec KV resident for the duration of a job, and the control API is where corpus-version invalidation of chunk KV should be wired in.

papers.title: Approximate Caching for Efficiently Serving Diffusion Models
papers.authors: Shubham Agarwal, Subrata Mitra, Sarthak Chakraborty, Srikrishna Karanam, Koyel Mukherjee, Shiv Kumar Saini
papers.citation_signal: NSDI 2024 (top networking/systems venue); Adobe Research; the paper the task scope refers to as 'approximate caching ... 2024' (misattributed there to Gill et al.); evaluated on real production prompt traces.
papers.key_contribution: Introduces approximate caching: for a new prompt, retrieve a semantically similar earlier prompt and reuse its intermediate noise state to skip part of the iterative denoising, with a cache policy, LCBFU (Least Computationally Beneficial and Frequently Used), that ranks entries by compute saved x reuse frequency. On two production workloads it reports 21% GPU compute savings, 19.8% end-to-end latency reduction and 19% dollar savings, plus a characterization of prompt popularity and reuse in production.
papers.design_implication: Two transferable ideas: (1) caching partial computation (intermediate states) rather than final outputs, which for LLM pipelines maps to caching retrieval results, reranker scores, partial plans and KV, with the final step still computed fresh; (2) a cost-benefit eviction score (compute saved x frequency) instead of recency, which the dossier only gestures at via RAGCache. Production prompt traces show heavy-tailed reuse, so eviction policy choice matters more than capacity.

papers.title: Semantic Data Caching and Replacement
papers.authors: Shaul Dar, Michael J. Franklin, Bjorn Thor Jonsson, Divesh Srivastava, Michael Tan
papers.citation_signal: The origin of the term and model of 'semantic caching' in databases; one of the most cited VLDB 1996 papers (well over a thousand citations) and the pre-LLM foundation the current semantic-caching literature re-derives.
papers.key_contribution: Proposes that a client cache track a semantic description of its contents (predicates over the data) rather than physical pages or tuple ids. A new query is split into a probe query answered from cache and a compact 'remainder query' sent to the server for only the missing part; usage statistics are kept per 'semantic region' and replacement uses semantic distance (e.g., Manhattan distance between query centers) rather than LRU. Shows semantic caching beats page- and tuple-based caching, especially under low bandwidth.
papers.design_implication: Two ideas the LLM semantic-caching literature lacks: (a) partial hits with remainder queries, i.e., when a cached answer covers part of a new question (same standard, different clause), reuse the covered part and call the LLM only for the remainder, which is exactly the decomposition the task-decomposition component can exploit; (b) describe cache contents by explicit predicates (document ids, clause ranges, requirement ids) so hit decisions can be exact on structure and approximate only on wording.

papers.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook
papers.authors: Rajesh Nishtala, Hans Fugal, Steven Grimm, Marc Kwiatkowski, Herman Lee, Harry C. Li, Ryan McElroy, Mike Paleczny, Daniel Peek, Paul Saab, David Stafford, Tony Tung, Venkateshwaran Venkataramani
papers.citation_signal: Canonical industrial caching paper (thousands of citations; taught in MIT 6.824 and most distributed-systems courses); the source of the 'lease' mechanism now in every large look-aside cache.
papers.key_contribution: Describes Facebook's look-aside cache serving billions of requests/second and the two consistency/overload problems it had to solve: stale sets (a slow client writing an outdated value after an invalidation) and thundering herds (many clients missing simultaneously on a hot invalidated key). Leases solve both: on a miss memcached hands the client a per-key token; a delete/invalidation voids outstanding tokens so late write-backs are rejected, and tokens are rate-limited so only the first missing client recomputes while others wait and retry the cache. Also covers invalidation pipelines (mcsqueal), regional pools, and cold-cluster warm-up.
papers.design_implication: The dossier's single-flight coalescing is half of the lease idea; the other half, token validation on write-back, is what prevents a dependency-based invalidation (document re-indexed) from being overwritten by an in-flight LLM call that started before the invalidation. Implement cache writes as 'set if lease still valid' and bump a per-key version on every purge; without this the invalidation layer has a race that re-installs stale grounded answers.

papers.title: SIEVE is Simpler than LRU: an Efficient Turn-Key Eviction Algorithm for Web Caches
papers.authors: Yazhuo Zhang, Juncheng Yang, Yao Yue, Ymir Vigfusson, K. V. Rashmi
papers.citation_signal: NSDI 2024 Community Award; companion to S3-FIFO (SOSP 2023, 'FIFO queues are all you need for cache eviction'); evaluated on 1,559 traces; implemented in five production cache libraries with <20 lines changed and adopted in dozens of open-source caches.
papers.key_contribution: Shows that a single FIFO queue with a moving 'hand' and one visited bit per object (lazy promotion, quick demotion) achieves lower miss ratios than LRU, ARC and other state-of-the-art policies on web and key-value workloads: up to 63.2% lower miss ratio than ARC, and lower miss ratio than nine SOTA algorithms on more than 45% of 1,559 traces. Cache hits need no locking, giving 2x the throughput of an optimized 16-thread LRU.
papers.design_implication: The dossier's eviction ladder (LRU -> ARC -> W-TinyLFU) omits the current simplest high-performing option. For the hot in-process exact-match layer and for embedding/retrieval result caches, SIEVE or S3-FIFO gives scan resistance and lock-free hits with almost no metadata; reserve W-TinyLFU for size-heterogeneous KV/response stores where admission matters. Choose by replaying your own trace, as the authors do with libCacheSim.

papers.title: Amortized Efficiency of List Update and Paging Rules
papers.authors: Daniel D. Sleator, Robert E. Tarjan
papers.citation_signal: Foundational competitive-analysis paper (thousands of citations); every online-algorithms textbook derives LRU's k-competitiveness from it.
papers.key_contribution: Introduces competitive analysis of online algorithms. For paging, proves that LRU's miss count on any sequence is within a factor dependent on fast-memory size k of Belady's offline MIN (k-competitive), and that no deterministic online paging algorithm can do better, so LRU is optimal among deterministic online policies in the worst case. Also shows move-to-front is within a constant factor of optimal for list update.
papers.design_implication: Completes the theory the dossier starts with Belady: the OPT gap you measure on traces is bounded by cache size in the worst case, and any gains from ARC/TinyLFU/SIEVE are workload-dependent, not worst-case. This justifies the dossier's 'measure the OPT gap on your own trace before switching policies' rule and warns against expecting a policy to fix a capacity problem.

papers.title: RFC 8785: JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS)
papers.authors: Anders Rundgren, Bret Jordan, Samuel Erdtman
papers.citation_signal: The IETF specification for canonical JSON hashing/signing; the dossier's exact-match technique says 'RFC 8785-style' without citing or describing it.
papers.key_contribution: Defines a deterministic serialization of I-JSON data for hashing and signing: object properties sorted recursively by UTF-16 code units, numbers serialized with the ECMAScript Number-to-string algorithm (so 1.0 and 1 serialize identically and no float-format ambiguity remains), minimal string escaping, no whitespace, UTF-8 output, no duplicate keys, NaN/Infinity rejected. Explicitly does not apply Unicode normalization.
papers.design_implication: Use JCS as the exact-match key serializer for structured request bodies (tool schemas, sampling params, CAD/BOM records), but note two consequences the dossier misses: Unicode NFC normalization must be a separate, explicit pre-step because JCS preserves strings byte-for-byte, and numeric canonicalization follows JavaScript semantics (large integers beyond 2^53 lose precision), so part numbers and ids must be strings, never numbers, in the key document.

papers.title: RFC 5861: HTTP Cache-Control Extensions for Stale Content
papers.authors: Mark Nottingham
papers.venue: IETF RFC 5861 (Informational); incorporated by reference in HTTP caching practice (RFC 9111)
papers.citation_signal: Implemented by every major CDN and HTTP cache (Fastly, Cloudflare, Varnish, nginx); the standard vocabulary for stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error that the dossier uses informally.
papers.key_contribution: Defines two cache directives: stale-while-revalidate=N lets a cache serve a stale response for up to N seconds while revalidating in the background without blocking the client; stale-if-error=N lets a cache serve a stale response when the origin returns 500/502/503/504 or is unreachable, up to a staleness bound, while still marking the response as stale.
papers.design_implication: Formalize the dossier's 'physical TTL longer than logical TTL' into two explicit per-profile parameters: a stale-while-revalidate window (serve the cached LLM answer immediately, enqueue an asynchronous regeneration, swap on completion) and a stale-if-error window (serve cached answers when the provider is rate-limiting or down). Both must be bounded by the caller's max_staleness and must surface the staleness in the response.

papers.title: Context caching (Gemini API documentation) and Gemini API pricing
papers.authors: Google
papers.citation_signal: Third major provider's prefix-caching contract; the only one with explicit, user-managed cache objects billed per token-hour, which breaks the dossier's claim that providers converge on one contract.
papers.key_contribution: Two modes: implicit caching (on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer; minimum 2,048 tokens for 2.5 Pro/Flash and 4,096 for the 3.x models listed; savings passed automatically; hit tokens reported in usage) and explicit caching (user creates a cache object with a TTL, default 1 hour, and references it; billed for creation plus storage per token-hour). Guidance: put large common content at the start and send similar-prefix requests close together.

Explicit caches pay off for long reference material (standards, specs) reused many times per hour, but an idle 1M-token cache costs $4.50/hour on 2.5 Pro, so TTL selection becomes a storage-budget decision and caches should be deleted at job end. The planner's break-even formula therefore needs provider-specific terms (write multiplier, read multiplier, storage rate, TTL).

papers.title: Context Caching / KV Cache on Disk (DeepSeek API documentation) and DeepSeek pricing

papers.citation_signal: Fourth provider contract and the most aggressive discount: automatic disk-based prefix caching with cache-hit input priced at roughly 2-3% of cache-miss input and no write surcharge.
papers.key_contribution: Caching is on by default for all users; every request builds a disk cache and later requests hit when they fully match a stored prefix unit (units are cut at request boundaries, at detected common prefixes, and at fixed intervals in long inputs). Only the input prefix is cached; outputs are generated fresh. Entries are cleared when unused, 'usually within a few hours to a few days'. Usage reports prompt_cache_hit_tokens and prompt_cache_miss_tokens. The cache planner should load these parameters from a per-provider table rather than hard-coding 1.25x/0.1x, and should treat 'unit boundaries' (DeepSeek) and 'breakpoints' (Anthropic/OpenAI GPT-5.6+) as adapter-specific ways to express the same prefix layout.

techniques.name: Canonical exact-match memoization with chained, versioned keys
techniques.description: (1) Normalize the request: Unicode NFC, trim and collapse whitespace, lowercase only where semantics permit (never inside code blocks, identifiers, part numbers), strip volatile fields (timestamps, request ids, trace ids) via an explicit allow-list of key-bearing fields. (2) Serialize the normalized request as canonical JSON (sorted keys, no insignificant whitespace, fixed float formatting). (3) Build the key as a hash chain, following vLLM's block-hash design: key = H(namespace || H(prev_segment) || H(this_segment) || extra_keys), where segments are the ordered prompt modules (tools, system, documents, user turn) and extra_keys include model id, prompt-template version, tool-schema hash, sampling parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, seed), retrieval corpus/snapshot version, embedding model id, and a tenant salt. (4) Store value plus metadata: created_at, last_hit_at, recompute_cost_ms (for XFetch), hit_count, verifier status, provenance (which document versions it depends on). (5) Lookup: exact key hit -> return; miss -> fall through to semantic/provider/engine layers.

techniques.when_to_use: Always, as the first layer: deterministic (temperature 0 or seeded) requests, idempotent tool calls, retrieval results, embeddings, reranker scores, and verified final answers.
techniques.tradeoffs: Zero false-hit risk and sub-millisecond lookups, but hit rates are low on free-form prompts unless normalization is good; over-aggressive normalization (e.g., lowercasing code) creates incorrect hits; forgetting a determinant in the key (model upgrade, tool schema change) serves stale/wrong outputs silently.
techniques.default_parameters: SHA-256 (vLLM default since v0.11; the docs warn non-cryptographic hashes risk collisions and cross-tenant leakage); include a per-tenant cache_salt; canonical JSON per RFC 8785-style sorted keys; only cache when temperature == 0 or a seed is set unless the task is explicitly diversity-tolerant (GPTCache's temperature knob, default 0.0). Version namespace format: {model_id}:{template_sha[:12]}:{tools_sha[:12]}:{corpus_version}.

techniques.name: Verified semantic caching with per-entry adaptive thresholds and exact-match guards
techniques.description: (1) Embed the normalized query (and, for multi-turn, a context chain: hash or embedding of the prior k turns, per MeanCache) with a domain-adapted embedding model. (2) ANN search (HNSW/IVF, cosine) for top-k candidates. (3) For each candidate, apply hard guards before similarity: identical normalized identifiers/numbers/units extracted by regex (part numbers, requirement ids, version strings, tolerances), identical task type, identical cache namespace (model, template, corpus version). (4) Decide hit using a per-entry threshold t_e learned online (vCache): maintain for each cached entry the observed similarity scores of accepted hits and whether they were later judged correct (by the verifier, user feedback, or sampled LLM-judge); choose t_e so the estimated error rate stays below the user-set budget delta. New entries start at a conservative global threshold. (5) On hit, return the cached response, record the similarity and outcome; on miss, call the LLM, store (embedding, response, metadata), and admit via the eviction/admission policy. (6) Periodically re-evaluate AUC on labeled 'same-answer' pairs; if AUC drops below target, retrain/distill the embedding (Zhu et al.) or switch to an ensemble.

techniques.when_to_use: Repetitive, paraphrase-heavy workloads (support/FAQ over standards and specs, 'what does clause X require', recurring incident triage questions) where MeanCache-style repeat rates (~31%) make the savings large and the answer is insensitive to wording. Not for generative/creative tasks or tasks whose answer depends on small numeric/identifier differences unless guards are in place.
techniques.tradeoffs: Up to 60-69% API-call reduction (GPT Semantic Cache) and 2-10x faster hits (GPTCache), but false hits are the dominant risk: general embeddings reach only AUC 0.51 on hard same-answer prediction (Zhu et al.), static thresholds give unpredictable error (vCache). Adds embedding latency (~ms) and vector-index memory; per-entry thresholds need feedback signals to converge.
techniques.default_parameters: Error budget delta = 1-2% for engineering/safety-relevant domains, up to 5% for low-stakes FAQ (vCache lets the operator pick; its experiments meet the chosen bound). Initial global cosine threshold conservative (>= 0.95 for general-purpose embeddings; GPTCache's example uses a distance threshold of 0.2) and tuned on labeled pairs to reach target precision; top-k = 5 candidates; context chain of the previous 2-3 turns (MeanCache); require AUC >= 0.8 on a held-out same-answer set before enabling in production (Zhu et al. reached 0.81 after fine-tuning); mismatch-cost weight per domain (Liu et al. 2025) with very high cost for numeric/identifier-bearing queries.

techniques.name: Provider prefix-cache layout optimizer (static-first ordering, breakpoints, TTL selection)
techniques.description: (1) Partition every request into ordered segments by volatility: tools -> system instructions -> long reference material (standards, spec sections, schemas, code files) -> conversation history -> current turn -> volatile context (timestamps, retrieved snippets that change per query). (2) Emit segments in exactly that order with byte-identical rendering (deterministic serialization of tool schemas, no reordering, no embedded timestamps or request ids in cached segments). (3) Place cache breakpoints (Anthropic: up to 4) at the end of the last stable block of each tier; rely on the automatic 20-position lookback for multi-turn growth and move the final breakpoint to the latest message each turn. (4) Choose TTL from the observed inter-arrival distribution of prefix reuse: 5-minute TTL (1.25x write) when reuse gaps are under 5 minutes; 1-hour TTL (2x write) when gaps are 5-60 minutes; for OpenAI, use prompt_cache_key per tenant/task to steer routing. (5) Gate: only attempt caching when the stable prefix exceeds the model's minimum (512-4,096 tokens on Anthropic; 1,024 on recent OpenAI models). (6) Warm-up: on a cold prefix, send one request and wait for its response to begin before fanning out parallel requests (the entry only becomes available after the first response begins). (7) Monitor cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read + cache_creation + input) as prefix hit ratio per template version.

techniques.when_to_use: Any hosted-API workload with long shared context: agent loops with large tool sets, document QA over standards/specs, multi-turn sessions, batch jobs over the same reference corpus.
techniques.tradeoffs: Reads cost 0.1x (down to 0.025-0.05x on newest models) with lower latency, but writes cost 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 h), so prefixes used once within TTL lose money; any upstream change (tool definition, image, thinking/effort, web-search toggle) invalidates downstream segments; summarization/compaction of history resets reuse; concurrency races on cold prefixes write the cache multiple times.
techniques.default_parameters: Break-even arithmetic from the documented multipliers: with 1.25x write and 0.1x read, N uses within TTL cost 1.25 + 0.1(N-1) vs N uncached, so caching wins from N=2; with the 2x 1-hour write it wins from N=3. Default TTL 5 minutes; promote a template to 1-hour TTL when its measured median reuse gap exceeds 5 minutes and expected reuses per hour >= 3. Minimum stable prefix: the model's documented minimum (512/1,024/2,048/4,096 tokens). Breakpoints: one at end of tools+system, one at end of reference material, one at the latest message. Fan-out: serialize the first call, then parallelize.

techniques.name: Engine-side KV reuse: radix/prefix caching, modular prompt caches, non-prefix fusion, shared-prefix batching
techniques.description: (1) Run a serving engine with automatic prefix KV caching (SGLang RadixAttention: radix tree keyed by token sequences with LRU leaf eviction and cache-aware scheduling; vLLM automatic prefix caching: block hashes chained from the parent block with extra keys and LRU free-queue eviction). (2) Register reusable prompt modules (system prompt, standard clauses, schemas, code files) so their KV can be precomputed and position-adjusted (Prompt Cache schema). (3) For RAG where retrieved chunks appear in varying positions, store per-chunk KV in a tiered store (GPU -> CPU -> SSD; RAGCache knowledge tree) and fuse at request time with selective recomputation of a small subset of tokens to restore cross-attention (CacheBlend), pipelining KV fetch with recompute; when KV must cross a network, compress and stream it adaptively (CacheGen). (4) Route requests sharing a prefix to the same engine and batch them so shared-prefix attention (Hydragen/ChunkAttention) is applied during decode. (5) Expose the engine's reported cached-token counts and TTFT as metrics; measure prefill vs decode share to know when KV reuse can help (it only speeds prefill).

techniques.when_to_use: Self-hosted or dedicated-capacity deployments with long shared contexts, heavy parallel sampling (self-consistency, decomposition fan-out), RAG with large retrieved contexts, or multi-tenant shared system prompts.
techniques.tradeoffs: Large TTFT/throughput gains (6.4x SGLang; 8x/60x Prompt Cache; 2.2-3.3x TTFT CacheBlend; up to 32x Hydragen at large batch; up to 4x TTFT RAGCache) with no quality loss when exact, but KV is memory-hungry (GB per long context), non-prefix reuse needs partial recompute to avoid quality loss, network transfer can erase savings without compression, and prefix caching does nothing for decode-dominated workloads.
techniques.default_parameters: Prefix caching always on (SGLang reports no measurable overhead without hits); vLLM block granularity of 16 tokens is the common configuration (docs illustrate 4 and 16; only full blocks are cached); sha256 hashing with cache_salt per tenant; LRU eviction at the engine (RadixAttention/vLLM default), promoted to cost-aware (recompute cost x frequency) at the tiered chunk store (RAGCache); CacheBlend-style partial recompute of a small fraction of tokens per fused chunk as the paper configures; apply Hydragen-style batching when batch size >= tens of sequences sharing >= 1K tokens of prefix (the paper shows gains grow with both).

techniques.name: Value-aware eviction and admission (LRU -> ARC/W-TinyLFU -> semantic cluster/mismatch-cost ranking), validated against Belady OPT
techniques.description: (1) Record every cache request (key, size, recompute cost, hit/miss) to a trace. (2) Replay the trace offline with Belady OPT to obtain the hit-rate upper bound for each capacity. (3) Start with LRU; if the OPT gap is material, switch the response cache to ARC (two LRU lists T1/T2 plus ghost lists B1/B2; ghost hits adapt the target size p of T1; scan-resistant, O(1)) or W-TinyLFU (small LRU admission window in front of a segmented-LRU main cache; a new item is admitted only if its TinyLFU sketch frequency exceeds the victim's; counters periodically halved for aging). (4) For semantic caches, rank entries by cluster value: tokens saved per hit x hit frequency (SCALM) minus expected mismatch cost (Liu et al. 2025); evict lowest-value entries and merge near-duplicate entries within a cluster. (5) Make eviction size-aware (bytes of response + embedding + KV) rather than entry-count-based. (6) Keep TTL as a separate correctness mechanism, not a substitute for eviction.

techniques.when_to_use: Whenever the cache is capacity-bound (always for KV; often for semantic indexes), the workload mixes hot repeated queries with one-off scans (batch log analysis, bulk document ingestion), or entries differ widely in recompute cost and size.
techniques.tradeoffs: ARC and W-TinyLFU add small metadata overhead (ghost lists, frequency sketch) but need no tuning and resist scans; semantic cluster ranking needs periodic re-clustering; cost-aware policies require accurate cost estimates. LRU remains adequate when the OPT gap is small.
techniques.default_parameters: Decision rule: adopt a smarter policy only if LRU's hit rate on trace replay is more than ~10 percentage points below Belady OPT at the deployed capacity. ARC: p initialized to 0, adapted by ghost hits as in the paper. W-TinyLFU: use the configuration in the TOS paper/Caffeine (small window ~1% of capacity feeding a segmented main region; 4-bit counters with periodic halving). SCALM-style semantic eviction: cluster-level frequency x tokens saved as the ranking score; GPTCache ships LRU/LFU/FIFO/RR, so plug in size-aware ARC or W-TinyLFU instead of its line-count eviction.

techniques.name: Stampede prevention and concurrent-miss coalescing (XFetch + single-flight + provider warm-up)
techniques.description: (1) Store with each cached entry its logical expiry and the measured recompute latency delta (ms). (2) On every read, recompute early if now - delta * beta * ln(rand()) >= expiry (rand uniform in (0,1], beta default 1.0); otherwise serve the cached value; set the physical TTL longer than the logical expiry so stale-while-revalidate is possible. (3) For cold misses, use single-flight coalescing: a per-key in-flight registry (local mutex or distributed lock/lease in Redis) so one request performs the LLM call while others await the same future; on provider prefix caches, send one request first and wait until its response begins before releasing the fan-out (Anthropic documents that the cache entry only becomes available after the first response begins). (4) Apply the same pattern to embedding and retrieval caches so a popular new query does not trigger N identical retrievals. (5) Emit metrics: coalesced requests, early refreshes, duplicate recomputes.

techniques.when_to_use: Any shared cache with hot keys (common questions, shared system prefixes, popular documents) and any pipeline stage that fans out parallel calls over a shared prefix.
techniques.tradeoffs: XFetch is lock-free and provably optimal but probabilistic (under very high concurrency two readers may still recompute); single-flight adds a small coordination cost and a failure mode if the leader dies (use leases with timeouts); serializing the warm-up call adds one request latency before fan-out.
techniques.default_parameters: beta = 1.0 (described as optimal for most cases in the paper's practitioner implementations); physical TTL = logical TTL + max expected recompute time; single-flight lease timeout = 2-3x p99 LLM latency; warm-up: block fan-out until the first response's message_start/first token arrives; negative caching of hard misses with TTL much shorter than positive TTL (RFC 2308's 1-3 hours works for DNS; for LLM pipelines bound negative TTL to minutes and to the corpus version).

techniques.name: Dependency-based invalidation and versioning (prompt, model, tool, corpus, verifier in the key; tag-based purge)
techniques.description: (1) Never mutate cache entries in place; invalidate by namespace: every determinant of the output (model id and provider, prompt-template content hash, tool/function schema hash, output schema, sampling params, embedding model id, reranker version, verifier version, corpus/index snapshot id) is part of the key, so a change naturally misses. (2) For fine-grained dependencies, store a tag set with each entry (document ids and versions it was grounded on, requirement ids, part numbers) in a secondary index; on document update or re-index, purge all entries tagged with that document (dependency-based invalidation), and bump the corpus snapshot id for coarse invalidation when many documents change. (3) Use TTL as a backstop for unknown dependencies (time-sensitive data, external tools), and expose the entry's age (staleness) alongside the answer so downstream components (verifier, UI) can decide to refresh. (4) For negative results, cache with a short TTL and the same tags so new documents become visible. (5) For provider prefix caches, treat tool-definition, image, thinking/effort and compaction changes as invalidation events and schedule them at session boundaries. (6) Log every invalidation cause for cost attribution.

techniques.when_to_use: Always; mandatory wherever cached outputs are grounded in mutable sources (requirements, standards revisions, incident databases, test logs, BOMs) or where models/prompts are iterated frequently.
techniques.tradeoffs: Including everything in the key lowers hit rate after each deploy (cold start); tag indexes add storage and write amplification; TTL alone cannot guarantee freshness, and overly long negative TTLs hide new data (RFC 2308 reports problems above one day).
techniques.default_parameters: Key namespace = {provider}:{model_id}:{template_sha}:{tools_sha}:{output_schema_sha}:{sampling_sig}:{corpus_snapshot}:{embedding_model}:{verifier_version}:{tenant}. Positive TTL: 24 h for grounded answers over versioned corpora (dependency purge handles correctness), 5-60 min for answers that include external/live tool data; negative TTL: 5-15 min. Record age_seconds on every hit and fail hits older than a per-task max_staleness configured by the caller.

techniques.name: Stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error serving tiers for LLM outputs
techniques.description: Store three timestamps per entry: fresh_until (logical TTL), swr_until = fresh_until + stale_while_revalidate, and sie_until = fresh_until + stale_if_error. On lookup: if now < fresh_until, serve. If fresh_until <= now < swr_until, serve the stale entry immediately with age_seconds and stale=true, and enqueue exactly one asynchronous regeneration (guarded by the single-flight lease) that replaces the entry when it completes and passes verification. If the upstream LLM call fails (429/5xx/timeout) and now < sie_until, serve the stale entry flagged stale_due_to_error; otherwise propagate the error. All windows are clipped by the caller's max_staleness; entries invalidated by dependency purge are exempt (purge deletes, it does not mark stale).

Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention
techniques.when_to_use: Interactive workloads where tail latency matters more than freshness by a few minutes (document QA over slowly-changing standards, FAQ over specs), and as the resilience layer when provider rate limits or outages occur.
techniques.tradeoffs: Hides provider failures and smooths p99 at the cost of serving slightly stale content; must never apply to answers whose dependencies were explicitly invalidated; background regeneration consumes budget even when no one re-asks, so bound it to keys with recent hit counts.
techniques.default_parameters: stale_while_revalidate = min(0.5 x TTL, 10 minutes) for grounded answers; stale_if_error = min(TTL, 1 hour); background refresh only for keys with >= 2 hits in the last TTL window; always return age_seconds and a stale flag; XFetch (beta = 1) for proactive refresh of hot keys remains the first line, SWR handles the keys XFetch missed.

techniques.name: Lease-validated cache writes (stale-set protection for dependency invalidation)
techniques.description: Every cache miss obtains a lease token (key, version, expiry) from the store before calling the LLM. Every invalidation (tag purge on document re-index, corpus snapshot bump, verifier version change) increments the key's version and voids outstanding leases. On write-back, the store accepts the value only if the lease is still valid (compare-and-set on version); otherwise the result is returned to the caller but not cached (or cached under the new version only if the caller re-validates its dependencies). Leases are rate-limited per key so only the first missing client recomputes while others wait for the lease holder (bounded wait) and then re-read; this is the lease form of single-flight coalescing that also works across processes.
source_titles: Scaling Memcache at Facebook
Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention
techniques.when_to_use: Any cache whose entries are grounded in mutable sources and whose fills take seconds (LLM calls), because the window between read-of-dependencies and write-of-result is long enough for an invalidation to land inside it.
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires an atomic version/CAS primitive in the store (Redis WATCH/MULTI or Lua, or a database row version); failed write-backs waste the LLM call; lease waits add latency for followers (bounded by lease timeout).
techniques.default_parameters: Lease TTL = 2-3x p99 LLM latency; one lease grant per key per lease TTL; follower wait = lease TTL then fall through to compute; version stored alongside tags so purge and version bump are one transaction.

techniques.name: Cache-aware distributed routing with load-aware replication (prefix-affinity scheduling)
techniques.description: Maintain a global index from prefix hash (per block/radix-node) to the set of engines/replicas whose KV store currently holds it, updated by engine eviction events. For each request, compute the longest cached prefix on each candidate engine; route to the engine maximizing (cached_prefix_tokens x prefill_cost_per_token - load_penalty(engine)). If the best engine's queue depth or memory exceeds a threshold, route to a less-loaded engine and let it compute (or fetch the KV from the holder when transfer is cheaper than recompute, per the CacheGen/Mooncake cost model), creating a replica of the prefix. Local schedulers then order queued requests by shared prefix to maximize radix hits within a batch.

Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation - A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (arXiv title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving)
LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs (RadixAttention)
techniques.when_to_use: Self-hosted deployments with more than one engine replica, fan-out workloads sharing long prefixes, and prefill/decode disaggregated clusters.
techniques.tradeoffs: Pure affinity creates hotspots when one prefix dominates (hence load-aware replication); the global index adds a lookup on the request path and must tolerate stale membership; KV transfer between engines needs bandwidth budgeting.
techniques.default_parameters: Prefer the holder of the longest prefix unless its load exceeds ~1.5x the fleet median (Preble uses a load-imbalance threshold with prefix-length-weighted scoring); re-evaluate placement every request; evict index entries on engine eviction callbacks; use transfer instead of recompute only when bytes/bandwidth < prefill time estimate.

techniques.name: Cross-turn session KV persistence with position-aware truncation
techniques.description: At the end of each turn, asynchronously save the session's KV blocks (layer by layer, overlapping with decode) to host memory, then to SSD or an external KV layer, indexed by (session id, model id, prefix hash chain). When the next turn is scheduled, pre-load the session KV layer-wise so the first layers compute while later layers stream in. When history must be truncated or compacted, truncate at block boundaries and decouple position encoding so retained KV remains valid (CachedAttention) or, if the engine cannot, treat compaction as a full invalidation and schedule it at turn boundaries where re-prefill is cheapest. Expose pin/unpin so long-running jobs keep their KV resident.
