LMCache: An Efficient KV Cache Layer for Enterprise-Scale LLM Inference
Mooncake: Trading More Storage for Less Computation - A KVCache-centric Architecture for Serving LLM Chatbot (arXiv title: Mooncake: A KVCache-centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving)
techniques.when_to_use: Agent loops and multi-turn engineering review sessions on self-hosted engines where inter-turn gaps exceed the engine's in-GPU cache residency.
techniques.tradeoffs: Host/SSD capacity and bandwidth; stale sessions must be evicted by idle time; truncation without position handling silently corrupts reuse; adds complexity relative to simply re-prefilling short histories.
techniques.default_parameters: Save to host DRAM after every turn, demote to SSD after ~5 minutes idle, evict after the session's expected return window (CachedAttention reports up to 87% TTFT reduction when the next turn hits host/disk tiers); block-aligned truncation; pin KV for jobs with known fan-out.

techniques.name: Partial-hit decomposition with remainder queries (semantic-region caching)
techniques.description: Describe each cached answer by an explicit coverage predicate (document ids and clause/section ranges, requirement ids, function/file ids) in addition to its embedding. On a new query, after retrieval identifies the needed coverage set, intersect it with cached predicates: fully covered sub-questions are served from cache; the uncovered remainder is sent to the LLM as a smaller query; the composed answer is returned and the remainder is cached with its own predicate. Replacement ranks semantic regions by usage and by distance from recent query centers rather than per-entry recency.
source_titles: Semantic Data Caching and Replacement
SCALM: Towards Semantic Caching for Automated Chat Services with Large Language Models
techniques.when_to_use: Structured reference corpora (standards, specs, requirement sets, codebases) where questions decompose along explicit structure and partial overlap between questions is common; pairs naturally with the task-decomposition component.
techniques.tradeoffs: Requires a decomposer that can split questions along coverage boundaries and a composer that can merge partial answers coherently; wrong predicates produce confident wrong hits, so predicates must come from retrieval/grounding metadata, not from the LLM's free text.
techniques.default_parameters: Only decompose when the uncovered remainder is <= 50% of the needed coverage (otherwise call the LLM once for the whole); predicates keyed by (corpus snapshot, document id, section id); region usage decays with the same aging as the frequency sketch.

techniques.name: FIFO-based lazy-promotion eviction (SIEVE / S3-FIFO) for hot lock-free layers
techniques.description: SIEVE: one FIFO queue plus a 'hand' pointer and a one-bit visited flag per object. On hit, set visited = 1 (no list movement, no lock). On eviction, advance the hand from tail toward head: objects with visited = 1 are reset to 0 and retained; the first object with visited = 0 is evicted; new objects insert at the head. S3-FIFO: a small FIFO (~10% of capacity) absorbs new arrivals; objects hit at least once while in the small queue are promoted to the main FIFO, others go to a ghost FIFO of keys; ghost hits re-admit to main. Both achieve quick demotion of one-hit wonders without LRU's per-hit metadata updates.
source_titles: SIEVE is Simpler than LRU: an Efficient Turn-Key Eviction Algorithm for Web Caches
TinyLFU: A Highly Efficient Cache Admission Policy
ARC: A Self-Tuning, Low Overhead Replacement Cache
techniques.when_to_use: The in-process exact-match layer and embedding/retrieval caches under high concurrency, and any cache where per-hit locking of an LRU list shows up in profiles; S3-FIFO when the workload has many one-hit wonders (bulk ingestion traffic).
techniques.tradeoffs: Not size-aware by default (combine with byte accounting); SIEVE can underperform on some block-storage-like traces where it is weaker than ARC; neither models recompute cost, so keep W-TinyLFU or cost-aware ranking for heterogeneous KV/response stores.
techniques.default_parameters: SIEVE: no parameters. S3-FIFO: small queue 10% of capacity, ghost queue sized to main-queue entry count. Validate by replaying your trace in libCacheSim-style simulation against LRU, ARC, W-TinyLFU and Belady OPT (SIEVE reports up to 63.2% lower miss ratio than ARC on web traces, 2x LRU throughput at 16 threads).

techniques.name: Tenant-scoped cache keys as a timing side-channel defense (cache-hit probing)
techniques.description: Prefix and KV caches leak information through latency: an attacker who can observe TTFT can test whether a given prefix (e.g., another tenant's system prompt or document) is cached. Mitigate by injecting a per-tenant or per-user salt into the first block's hash (vLLM cache_salt) so only requests with the same salt can hit; on hosted APIs use per-customer prompt_cache_key (OpenAI documents that the key on GPT-5.6+ helps prevent cache-hit probing across users) and rely on organization/workspace isolation (Anthropic). Never share semantic-cache indexes across tenants, add jitter or coarse quantization to any externally visible cache-hit indicator, and audit which tenant each cached object was served to.

techniques.when_to_use: Any multi-tenant deployment, any cache shared across users within a tenant where prompts can contain confidential data, and self-hosted engines exposed to multiple teams.
techniques.tradeoffs: Salting fragments the cache and lowers hit rates (shared public reference material should use a shared salt scope, private material a per-user scope); jittering hit indicators complicates latency SLO reporting.
techniques.default_parameters: Two salt scopes: 'shared-reference' (public standards, model-wide system prompts) and 'tenant-private' (everything containing user or project data); salt = HMAC(tenant_id, secret); per-user prompt_cache_key on OpenAI; cryptographic hash (sha256) for all keys; log (tenant, key namespace, hit/miss) for audit.

techniques.name: JCS canonicalization with explicit normalization and numeric-safety rules for exact keys
techniques.description: Build the exact-match key document as I-JSON with all identifiers, part numbers, versions and tolerances encoded as strings; apply Unicode NFC and the allow-listed field projection first (JCS does not normalize Unicode and rejects duplicate keys); serialize with RFC 8785 (recursive key sort by UTF-16 code units, ECMAScript number formatting, no whitespace, UTF-8); then hash with SHA-256 chained over ordered prompt modules. Reject documents containing NaN/Infinity or integers above 2^53 at build time. Pin the serializer version in the key namespace so a serializer change is an explicit invalidation.

techniques.when_to_use: Always for the exact-match layer, for tool-schema and output-schema hashing, and for CAD/BOM/requirements records serialized into prompts.
techniques.tradeoffs: JCS numeric rules follow JavaScript (precision loss beyond 2^53, 1.0 == 1), which is desirable for sampling params but dangerous for ids; the extra normalization pass costs microseconds; different-language implementations must be conformance-tested against the RFC test vectors.
techniques.default_parameters: Serializer id in namespace (e.g., jcs-v1); NFC before JCS; strings for all ids; SHA-256; vLLM's default sha256 path uses pickle and is documented as not reproducible across Python/vLLM versions, so for any persisted or externally shared KV key use a stable byte-level encoding of token ids, not the engine's in-memory hash.

architecture_recommendations: 1. Build the component as a layered cache policy engine with four pluggable layers behind one interface (lookup/put/invalidate/stats): L1 exact-match memoization (in-process LRU + Redis), L2 verified semantic cache (vector index + scalar store + per-entry thresholds), L3 provider prefix-cache layout optimizer (Anthropic/OpenAI adapters), L4 engine KV reuse hooks (SGLang/vLLM/LMCache). Each layer is independently enableable per task via configuration, and each reports its own hit/miss/cost metrics.

2. Give the component a 'cache planner' that reasons over the incoming natural-language task prompt plus declared metadata: it classifies the task (lookup vs generative, deterministic vs diverse, grounded vs ungrounded, numeric/identifier-sensitive or not), estimates reuse probability from historical trace statistics for the template, and emits a cache plan: which layers to consult, the semantic error budget, TTLs, the prefix layout and breakpoints, and whether to warm the provider cache before fan-out. The planner itself should be a cheap deterministic rule engine with an optional small-model fallback, and its decisions must be logged.

3. Make key construction a single shared library implementing the vLLM-style hash chain (namespace || parent hash || segment hash || extra keys) with SHA-256 and a per-tenant cache_salt, so exact, semantic, prefix and KV layers all agree on what determines an output. Every determinant (model, template version, tool schema, output schema, sampling parameters, corpus snapshot, embedding model, verifier version) is part of the namespace; forgetting one is the main way caches serve wrong answers.

4. Implement the semantic layer as a verified cache: configurable error budget per task family, per-entry thresholds learned online from verifier/user feedback (vCache), hard exact-match guards on extracted identifiers, numbers and units, context-chain keys for multi-turn (MeanCache), and a quarterly AUC regression on labeled same-answer pairs (Zhu et al.). Store embeddings in an in-memory ANN index (HNSW/Redis) and responses in a durable store; keep the embedding model id in the key namespace so model swaps invalidate cleanly.

5. Treat prompt assembly as a cache-aware compiler stage: a template registry of named, versioned, byte-stable modules (tools, system, reference material, history, turn) rendered in volatility order with deterministic serialization; breakpoints emitted per provider; forbidden-content linting (timestamps, request ids, nondeterministic ordering inside cached segments); and a per-template dashboard of prefix hit ratio computed from cache_read_input_tokens.

6. Provide a tiered store abstraction for large values (KV tensors, long responses): GPU/CPU/SSD/object storage with cost-aware eviction (recompute cost x frequency, RAGCache), compression for cross-node transfer (CacheGen), and an admission filter (W-TinyLFU) so one-off requests do not displace hot entries. Eviction must be size-aware in bytes, not entry counts (the documented GPTCache OOM pitfall).

7. Build concurrency controls in from the start: single-flight coalescing of identical in-flight misses (local and distributed lease), XFetch probabilistic early refresh for hot keys with the measured recompute latency stored per entry, and provider-cache warm-up that serializes the first request before parallel fan-out.

8. Implement invalidation as namespaced versioning plus dependency tags: each entry carries the document/requirement/part ids and versions it was grounded on; ingestion and re-index events purge by tag and bump the corpus snapshot; TTL is a backstop; negative results are cached briefly; every hit returns age_seconds and provenance so the verifier and UI can enforce max_staleness.

9. Expose configuration as a declarative per-domain profile (YAML/JSON): layers enabled, error budget, similarity guards (regex sets for identifiers/units), TTLs, max_staleness, eviction policy, capacity, provider adapters, tenant isolation. Ship profiles for 'engineering-strict' (semantic delta <= 1%, numeric/identifier guards on, 1-hour prefix TTL for standards), 'support-FAQ' (delta <= 5%), and 'generative' (semantic cache off, exact cache only with seed).

10. Instrument for evaluation and safety: per-layer hit rate, false-hit rate (sampled verifier/LLM-judge), tokens and dollars saved (using documented provider multipliers), p50/p99 TTFT and end-to-end latency with and without cache, staleness distribution, invalidation causes, coalesced requests, and offline trace replay against Belady OPT. Support shadow mode (compute hits but do not serve them) for safe rollout of new thresholds or embeddings.

11. Enforce tenant and privacy boundaries: separate namespaces/salts per tenant, no cross-tenant semantic matching, optional user-side or federated similarity-model training for sensitive domains (MeanCache), and audit logs of which cached response was served to whom.

12. Keep the component pipeline-pluggable through middleware semantics: it wraps any 'call' (LLM, embedding, retrieval, rerank, tool) with the same interface, accepts a task context object from the orchestrator (task id, decomposition node id, verification status), and emits events so the decomposition, verification and parallelization components can request warm-up, mark entries verified, or purge on dependency change.

Cache poisoning and prompt-injection amplification: a semantic or exact cache turns one bad generation into many served answers. Treat admission as a security boundary: only admit responses that passed the verifier (or were produced from inputs that passed injection screening), store the provenance of every retrieved chunk that influenced the response, support purge-by-source when a document is later found to contain injected instructions, and never admit responses produced while a tool call returned untrusted content unless the verifier approved them. Shadow mode plus sampled human review is the detection path.

Cache-hit timing side channels: both vLLM (cache_salt rationale) and OpenAI (prompt_cache_key on GPT-5.6+ 'helps prevent cache-hit probing across users') document that prefix caches leak membership via latency. Add per-tenant/per-user salts, never share semantic indexes across tenants, and avoid exposing raw hit/miss or TTFT per request to end users where prompts contain confidential data.

Observability: emit per-namespace (provider, model, template version, tenant) counters for cache_creation vs cache_read tokens, write-amplification ratio (writes with zero subsequent reads within TTL), semantic false-hit rate from sampled verification, staleness histogram, invalidation causes, lease waits and failed write-backs, and 'cold-prefix races' (multiple cache_creation events for the same prefix hash within one TTL). Alert when write-amplification exceeds ~50% for a template, since that indicates volatile content before the breakpoint.

Cost control with provider-specific economics: implement the break-even calculator as a table-driven function of (write multiplier, read multiplier, storage rate per token-hour, TTL, expected reuses) loaded per provider and model, because the inputs range from 1.25x/0.1x (Anthropic, OpenAI GPT-5.6+) to no-write-charge/24h (older OpenAI), 0.1x plus $1-$4.50 per 1M tokens per hour (Gemini explicit caches) and ~0.025x (DeepSeek, newest Claude models). For Gemini explicit caches, delete cache objects at job end and budget storage-hours explicitly.

Failure handling: wrap the cache store (Redis/vector index) in a circuit breaker so store outages degrade to cache-bypass rather than request failure; implement stale-if-error so provider 429/5xx can be absorbed from cache within a bounded staleness; make lease timeouts and background refresh idempotent; and record that the Batches API on Anthropic offers only best-effort hits (the docs recommend a single 1-hour-cache warm-up request before submitting the batch).

Hash and serializer stability as part of the key contract: pin the serializer version (JCS), tokenizer version and hashing scheme in the namespace. Engine-internal hashes (vLLM's pickle-based sha256) are documented as not reproducible across versions, so persisted KV indexes must key on a stable byte encoding of token ids plus model id, and tokenizer upgrades must be treated as invalidation events.

Session-level KV persistence and compaction policy for self-hosted engines: adopt CachedAttention-style save/pre-load of session KV across idle turns with block-aligned, position-aware truncation, and make compaction a scheduled event at turn boundaries (mirroring the provider-side guidance that compaction resets reuse). Expose pin/unpin on the KV layer (LMCache control APIs) so long fan-out jobs keep their reference-material KV resident.

Distributed cache-aware routing: for multi-replica self-hosting implement Preble-style prefix-affinity scheduling (global prefix hash -> holder map, load-aware replication threshold) and a transfer-vs-recompute cost model (Mooncake/CacheGen) rather than the dossier's informal 'route to the same engine'.

Evaluation methodology: build a trace-replay harness (libCacheSim-style) that replays recorded (key, size, recompute cost, dependency tags) traces against LRU, ARC, W-TinyLFU, SIEVE/S3-FIFO, cost-aware ranking and Belady OPT at several capacities, and a semantic benchmark suite that includes the four vCache benchmarks plus domain-labeled same-answer pairs with adversarial near-duplicates (identifiers, units, tolerances changed). Report per-layer hit rate, false-hit rate under the error budget, and quality parity with confidence intervals; require shadow-mode results before enabling any new threshold, embedding or eviction policy.

Partial-hit reuse: integrate the task-decomposition component with the cache so that sub-questions already answered for the same (document, section, version) are served from cache and only the remainder is sent to the LLM (Dar et al. remainder queries); this typically yields more savings on structured engineering corpora than raising the semantic similarity hit rate.
pitfalls: Semantic false hits from similarity-vs-equivalence confusion: general embeddings predict 'same answer' at chance level (AUC 0.51) on hard pairs (Zhu, Zhu & Jiao 2024); static thresholds give unpredictable error rates (vCache, Schroeder et al. 2025). Mitigate with per-entry adaptive thresholds under an explicit error budget, domain fine-tuned or ensemble embeddings, exact-match guards on identifiers/numbers, and sampled verification of hits.

Context-blind semantic hits in multi-turn use: follow-up queries ('and for the next clause?') match unrelated cached entries without context (MeanCache, Gill et al. 2024). Mitigate by including a context chain in the semantic key and separating standalone from contextual queries.

Non-prefix KV reuse that ignores cross-attention: reusing precomputed KV for chunks that are not a prefix silently degrades generation quality unless a subset of tokens is recomputed (CacheBlend, Yao et al. 2024). Mitigate with selective recompute/fusion or by restricting KV reuse to true prefixes.

Prefix-cache invalidation by unnoticed upstream changes: tool-definition edits invalidate the entire cache, image add/remove invalidates tools+system, thinking/effort and web-search/citation toggles invalidate message blocks, and compaction/summarization resets reuse (Anthropic and OpenAI prompt-caching docs). Mitigate with byte-stable rendering, change linting, scheduling such changes at session boundaries, and monitoring cache_read ratio per template.

Volatile content inside the cached prefix (timestamps, request ids, user input before the breakpoint) writes a fresh entry each request and never hits, incurring 1.25-2x write cost for nothing (Anthropic docs). Mitigate by placing dynamic content after the last breakpoint and linting templates.

Cold-prefix concurrency: parallel requests sent before the first response begins each pay the cache-write price and get no hit (Anthropic docs). Mitigate by serializing a warm-up request before fan-out.

Cache stampede / thundering herd on hot expired keys causing bursts of expensive LLM recomputation (Vattani, Chierichetti & Lowenstein 2015). Mitigate with XFetch probabilistic early expiration (beta=1) and single-flight coalescing.

Cross-tenant leakage and hash collisions when using non-cryptographic hashes or shared namespaces (vLLM prefix-caching design docs). Mitigate with SHA-256 keys, per-tenant cache_salt, and strict namespace isolation; never do semantic matching across tenants.
Entry-count eviction leading to OOM because values (long responses, embeddings, KV tensors) vary widely in size (GPTCache README). Mitigate with byte-aware capacity accounting and tiered storage.

Scan pollution: bulk one-off queries (batch log triage, ingestion-time summarization) flush hot entries under plain LRU (ARC, Megiddo & Modha 2003; TinyLFU, Einziger et al. 2017). Mitigate with ARC or W-TinyLFU admission, or a separate namespace for batch traffic.

Overly long negative caching hides newly available data; RFC 2308 reports problems with negative TTLs over one day. Mitigate with short negative TTLs tied to corpus versions and tag-based purge on ingestion.

Serving stale grounded answers after the underlying document, requirement or BOM changes when only TTL governs freshness (RAGCache/CacheBlend motivate versioned KV; provider docs show caches are content-addressed, not dependency-aware). Mitigate with dependency tags, corpus snapshot ids in the key, and age/provenance returned with every hit.

Caching nondeterministic or diversity-requiring outputs (sampling at temperature > 0, brainstorming) collapses variety and can serve one unlucky sample forever (GPTCache's temperature bypass exists for this reason). Mitigate by caching only seeded/temperature-0 calls or storing multiple samples per key.

Expecting prefix/KV caching to speed decode-dominated workloads: it reduces only prefill time (vLLM automatic-prefix-caching docs). Mitigate by measuring prefill vs decode share before investing, and using shared-prefix batching (Hydragen) for decode-heavy fan-out.

KV transfer over the network erasing savings for distributed caches (CacheGen, Liu et al. 2024). Mitigate with KV compression/streaming and a cost model that falls back to recompute when bandwidth is poor.

Evaluating only on synthetic or FAQ-like data: several semantic-caching results (e.g., Liu et al. 2025's synthetic evaluation; GPT Semantic Cache's customer-service queries) may not transfer to engineering text with dense identifiers. Mitigate with domain trace replay, labeled same-answer sets, and shadow-mode rollout.
evaluation_metrics: Per-layer hit rate (exact, semantic, provider prefix, engine KV) and overall request-level hit rate; provider prefix hit ratio = cache_read_input_tokens / (cache_read + cache_creation + input tokens) per template version (Anthropic/OpenAI usage fields)

Semantic false-hit rate (incorrect served hits / served hits), precision, recall and F-score of hit/miss decisions on labeled same-answer pairs, and AUC of the similarity score as a cache-validity predictor (MeanCache, Zhu et al., vCache benchmarks); target AUC >= 0.8 and error <= configured budget
Positive hit rate from sampled verifier/LLM-judge or user feedback on served hits (GPT Semantic Cache reports >97%)
Cost saved: tokens avoided and dollars saved computed with documented multipliers (uncached vs 1.25x/2x write and 0.1x read), including write amplification cost of never-hit prefixes

Latency: p50/p95/p99 time-to-first-token and end-to-end latency on hits vs misses, and TTFT reduction factor for KV reuse (literature baselines: 2-10x GPTCache hits; 2.2-3.3x CacheBlend; up to 4x RAGCache)
Throughput (requests/s or tokens/s) under shared-prefix batching, versus baseline (SGLang up to 6.4x; Hydragen up to 32x at large batch)

Staleness: distribution of age_seconds of served entries, fraction of hits exceeding task max_staleness, time-to-visibility of new documents after ingestion (negative-cache and dependency-purge effectiveness)
Eviction quality: hit rate versus Belady OPT on recorded traces at deployed capacity; admission rejection rate; bytes evicted per hour
Concurrency health: coalesced duplicate misses, duplicate recomputes, early-refresh count (XFetch), stampede incidents
Storage and memory footprint per entry (response bytes, embedding bytes, KV bytes) and tier residency (GPU/CPU/SSD) for KV caches; KV compression ratio where streaming is used (CacheGen 3.5-4.3x)
Invalidation accounting: invalidations by cause (model/template/tool/corpus/verifier change, TTL expiry, tag purge) and resulting cold-start hit-rate dip
Quality parity: task accuracy on cached vs uncached paths on the pipeline's own evaluation set (must be statistically indistinguishable for exact/KV layers)
engineering_adaptation_notes: Code: never lowercase or whitespace-normalize inside code for exact keys; hash the AST or token stream of the file version plus language/toolchain version; cache per-file analyses (summaries, symbol tables, embeddings) keyed by content hash so unchanged files across commits hit; semantic caching of code questions must guard on symbol names, file paths and version strings, which embeddings blur.

Specifications and standards: these are long, stable, and reused across many queries, so they are ideal for 1-hour provider prefix caching and engine-side KV reuse; register each standard/spec section as a named prompt module with a content hash and revision id; invalidate by revision; cache 'which clause applies' answers with dependency tags on clause ids.

Requirements: requirement ids (e.g., REQ-1234) and verification status are exact-match guards; semantic hits must require identical requirement ids and baseline/version; include the requirements-baseline id in the namespace so a baseline change purges derived answers (traceability matrices, impact analyses).

Incident reports and test logs: high churn and timestamp-heavy; strip timestamps, host names, run ids and counters before hashing to expose true repeats (same failure signature); cache classification/triage outputs keyed by normalized failure signature; use negative caching for 'no known matching incident' with short TTL so new incidents become visible; prefer exact/normalized-match over semantic caching because near-identical logs with one differing error code must not collide.

CAD/BOM metadata: structured records serialize deterministically to canonical JSON (sorted keys, fixed numeric formatting, units normalized); part numbers, revisions and quantities are exact-match guards; numeric tolerances ('5 mm' vs '50 mm') defeat embedding similarity, so semantic caching for BOM/CAD questions should use an 'engineering-strict' profile (error budget <= 1%, numeric guards on) or be disabled in favor of exact keys.

Mismatch cost is domain-specific and high: configure the semantic layer's mismatch cost (Liu et al. 2025) far above FAQ defaults for safety-relevant or compliance answers, and route such hits through the verification component before serving.

Determinism and auditability: engineering workflows need reproducibility, so cache only seeded/temperature-0 generations for design or compliance outputs, store provenance (document versions, model id, template version) with every entry, and surface age and provenance to the user.

Multi-tenant/IP isolation: separate namespaces and salts per program, supplier or classification level; semantic matching must never cross these boundaries; consider user-side or federated similarity-model training (MeanCache) where prompts contain proprietary design data.
composition_notes: Hybrid retrieval: cache query embeddings, BM25/vector result lists and reranker scores keyed by (normalized query hash, index snapshot id, retriever/reranker version); cache the retrieved chunks' KV states in a tiered store (RAGCache) and fuse non-prefix chunks with CacheBlend-style partial recompute so chunk order need not be frozen for hits; purge retrieval-derived entries by document tag on re-index.

Task decomposition: memoize each DAG node (sub-task prompt + inputs) with exact keys so repeated or overlapping sub-tasks across plans hit; keep the planner/system prompt a byte-stable shared prefix so all sub-task calls reuse the provider prefix cache or the radix KV tree (RadixAttention is designed for such tree-structured programs); the decomposer can emit cache hints (expected reuse, staleness tolerance) with each node.

Answer verification: the verifier is the feedback signal that lets the semantic cache learn per-entry thresholds under an error budget (vCache); cache only verified answers (or store verification status with the entry) and invalidate when the verifier version changes; cache verifier verdicts themselves keyed by (answer hash, evidence hash); treat a verifier rejection as a negative-cache entry with short TTL.

Parallelization: group fan-out calls by prefix hash so they land in the same engine batch (Hydragen/ChunkAttention shared-prefix attention) or hit the same provider prefix entry; serialize one warm-up call before fan-out because provider cache entries become available only after the first response begins; use single-flight coalescing so parallel workers issuing identical sub-queries share one LLM call; self-consistency sampling should reuse one cached prefix and cache the aggregated (voted) answer, not individual samples, unless diversity is required.

Pipeline RAG: apply caching at every stage (embedding, retrieval, rerank, context assembly, generation, verification) with a shared key library and corpus snapshot id; order the generation prompt as system -> stable reference docs -> retrieved chunks -> query so prefix caching covers the static part and KV chunk caching covers the dynamic part; monitor stage-wise hit rates and TTFT to find the dominant cost.

Prompting and architecture best practices: static-first prompt layout and template registries (Prompt Cache modules) are both a caching and a prompt-engineering discipline; avoid embedding timestamps or run ids in system prompts; make tool schemas and output schemas versioned and byte-stable; schedule history compaction deliberately because it resets provider prefix reuse (OpenAI docs); keep a temperature/seed policy per task so the exact cache knows what is cacheable.
critique_corrections: Claim (Anthropic entry and pitfalls): 'image changes invalidate tools+system'. The documentation's invalidation table says the opposite: for images, tools and system caches are preserved and only message blocks are invalidated ('Adding/removing images anywhere in the prompt affects message blocks'). Correct statement: images invalidate message-block caches only.

Claim (pitfalls): 'web-search/citation toggles invalidate message blocks'. The docs table shows enabling/disabling web search or citations modifies the system prompt, invalidating both the system cache and the message cache (tools preserved). The dossier understates the blast radius.

Claim: 'thinking/effort settings invalidate message blocks'. The docs say changing thinking parameters 'always invalidates message blocks; tool and system caches are also invalidated on models that render the configuration ahead of them', and that output_config.effort behaves the same way; tool_choice changes and speed-setting changes also invalidate message blocks. The dossier should list these and note the model-dependent system/tool invalidation.

Claim: 'the system automatically looks back up to 20 block positions per breakpoint'. The docs state it 'checks at most 20 positions per breakpoint, counting the breakpoint itself as the first', and that a run of consecutive tool_use blocks (or tool_result blocks) counts as one position; so for agent loops the effective lookback in content blocks is larger than 20 and the count is 19 before the breakpoint.

Claim (SCALM entry): 'venue not confirmed on arXiv page'. The venue is confirmed: IEEE Xplore document 10682957, 2024 IEEE/ACM 32nd International Symposium on Quality of Service (IWQoS), DOI 10.1109/IWQoS61813.2024.10682957. Update the venue field.

Claim (Belady entry): the URL given is https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A1szl%C3%B3_B%C3%A9l%C3%A1dy, a biography page, not the paper. The bibliographic record (IBM Systems Journal 5(2):78-101, 1966) is confirmed by the Silberschatz OS bibliography (os-book.com/OS10/bib-dir/10.pdf); cite that or the IBM/IEEE DOI record instead of Wikipedia.

Claim (Vattani entry): URL is an institutional repository handle (iris.uniroma1.it). The canonical open PDF is https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p886-vattani.pdf (PVLDB vol. 8, starting p. 886, consistent with the dossier's 8(8):886-897). Prefer the VLDB Endowment URL.

Claim (OpenAI entry / technique 3): 'Both major providers converge on the same contract (exact prefix, static-first, ~1.25x write/0.1x read)'. This holds only for Anthropic and for OpenAI GPT-5.6+. OpenAI's earlier models have no cache-write surcharge and offer in_memory (5-10 min, up to 1 h) or 24h retention (default 24h for non-ZDR orgs); explicit breakpoints exist only on GPT-5.6+ and the only TTL value is 30m. Gemini bills explicit caches per token-hour of storage ($4.50/1M tokens/hour on 2.5 Pro, $1.00 on 2.5 Flash) with 0.1x cached input and a default 1-hour TTL. DeepSeek charges ~0.02-0.03x for cache-hit input with no write surcharge and keeps entries for hours to days. The planner's break-even arithmetic must be per-provider.

Claim (Anthropic entry): read multipliers '0.05x and 0.025x on the newest models' is confirmed (Opus 5.5/Sonnet 5.5 at 0.05x; Fable 5.1/Mythos 5.1 at 0.025x), but the dossier's break-even statement 'the 1-hour TTL (2x write) pays off from the third use' assumes 0.1x reads; at 0.025x reads the 1-hour write still needs N=3 (2 + 0.025 = 2.025 > 2 at N=2) so the conclusion stands, while the 5-minute case saves 0.875 instead of 0.65 of a base call at N=2. State the multiplier the arithmetic assumes.

Claim (vLLM entry / technique 1): presents 'sha256 default since v0.11' as a stable, canonical key. The vLLM design doc adds that the default sha256 path 'uses Python's pickle' and 'Hashes may not be reproducible across different Python or vLLM versions', and offers xxhash/xxhash_cbor as non-cryptographic alternatives with an explicit collision/multi-tenant leakage warning. For any KV or key persisted outside one engine process (LMCache tiers, external stores), the dossier should require a version-stable encoding rather than the engine's in-memory hash.

Claim (vLLM entry): 'prefix caching speeds only prefill ... per the vLLM design docs'. That statement is in the vLLM features page (automatic_prefix_caching: 'APC only reduces the time of processing the queries (the prefilling phase)... does not reduce the time of generating new tokens'), not the design/prefix_caching page, which contains the hash-chain and eviction description. Minor attribution fix.

Claim (CacheBlend entry): 'implemented in LMCache, which is reported as the KV caching layer used with Red Hat, IBM, Google and CoreWeave deployments'. The EuroSys 2025 Best Paper award is confirmed (UChicago CS news and LMCache announcement), but the adoption list originates from the University of Chicago's own press release and is not independently verified; label it as a self-reported claim.

Claim (task scope, repeated in the dossier framing): 'approximate caching by Gill et al. 2024'. The 'Approximate Caching' paper (NIRVANA) is by Agarwal, Mitra, Chakraborty, Karanam, Mukherjee and Saini (Adobe Research/UIUC), NSDI 2024, arXiv 2312.04429, and concerns text-to-image diffusion models; Gill et al. 2024 is MeanCache. The dossier correctly omits a Gill 'approximate caching' paper but should include the Agarwal paper under its correct attribution.

Claim (Hydragen entry): 'the shared-prefix attention decomposition it introduced is now used in production attention kernels' and the citation count are unverified in any source checked; the venue (ES-FoMo-II workshop at ICML 2024, OpenReview id Ye3ia34Fpp, poster) is confirmed. Also note the workshop version reports 'over 3x at 1K prefix and over 30x at 16K prefix' while the arXiv abstract says 'up to 32x'; both are consistent but the dossier should say the 32x figure is at batch 1K with a 16K shared prefix.

Claim (GPTCache entry): 'similarity_threshold ... exposes a configurable similarity_threshold'. The README shows similarity_threshold only in a commented-out example (Config(similarity_threshold=0.2)) and gives no default or range; the only documented knob with range and default is temperature ([0, 2], default 0.0). The 8.2k star count and the entry-count ('number of lines') eviction/OOM caveat are confirmed on the repository page.
